paper.paper_title: EEGNet: A Compact Convolutional Network for EEG-based Brain-Computer Interfaces
paper.paper_abstract: EEGNet is a compact convolutional network for EEG-based brain-computer interfaces. It uses depthwise and separable convolutions to represent EEG feature extraction concepts. The study compares it with reference approaches across P300, error-related negativity, movement-related cortical potentials, and sensory motor rhythms. With limited training data, it generalizes across paradigms better than the reference algorithms. The authors also visualize learned features to investigate their interpretation. This is a paraphrase of the arXiv abstract, not the full paper or a verbatim abstract.

paper.paper_title: RL Post-Training in Diffusion Transformers Is Activation Steering
paper.paper_abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training substantially improves the visual quality, text rendering, and compositional accuracy of diffusion transformers. Because capabilities such as rendering requested text or composing multiple objects are inherently prompt-dependent, a natural hypothesis is that improving them requires learning complex, input-dependent transformations. To isolate how much of these gains an input-independent shift explains, we probe each RL-tuned model with a deliberately simple parameterization: a fixed set of steering vectors added to the block outputs of the frozen base model. On SD3.5-M, these vectors hold 65x fewer parameters than the RL-tuned LoRA (0.29M against 18.8M). We fit them to match the velocity predictions of public RL-tuned checkpoints, with no reward in the objective. Although the vectors are identical for every prompt, token, and sampling seed, they recover 90.0-96.3% of the reward gains of six RL-tuned image models, and 89.8% and 111.9% on two RL-tuned video models. Initialized at zero and trained with online RL, the vectors alone exceed the reward gains of weight-based RL on text rendering (OCR) and human preference (PickScore) on SD3.5-M. A constant shift thus suffices for most of the gain of policy-gradient RL post-training: without new input-dependent transformations, it steers the pretrained generator toward what it can already compute.

paper.paper_title: TideCache: Efficient Hybrid LLM Serving with Transparent Cache Management and Layer-Wise Streaming
paper.paper_abstract: Hybrid architectures have become mainstream among open-weight language models. Their global-attention and bounded-state layers maintain heterogeneous caches whose demands vary with context length and concurrency. We present TideCache, a serving system on CPU--GPU superchips with three components for allocating GPU memory among caches and managing their residency across GPU and host memory. The Transparent Cache Pool redistributes physical pages among cache components behind fixed virtual addresses, preserving cache layouts and backend interfaces. The Cache Streamer uses computation intervals provided by bounded-state layers to prefetch the next global-attention layer's prefix into GPU slots shared across global-attention layers, reducing GPU residency while overlapping layer-wise transfers with computation. Generated KV remains resident. The Request Scheduler selects resident or streamed execution and triggers capacity adjustments according to request size and queue state. Together, they let HBM released by streaming accommodate other cache components and additional requests. Implemented in SGLang and evaluated on GB300 and GH200 across seven model/platform configurations, TideCache completes up to 2.04x as many agent turns, reduces overall P50 per-token latency by 20--59%, and improves agent P50 TTFT by 1.40--3.05x compared with SGLang with HiCache.

paper.paper_title: One Prior, Two Dynamics: Repurposing Video Diffusion Transformers for Self-Supervised Latent Action Learning
paper.paper_abstract: Videos reveal how the world changes, but rarely the actions that cause those changes. Latent action learning recovers such supervision from visual transitions, yet often learns the underlying dynamics largely from scratch. We ask whether a pretrained video generator can instead provide the prior for both inverse and forward dynamics. We introduce O$^{2}$LaF, built on a simple principle: one prior, two dynamics. We initialize both models from the same pretrained video DiT and adapt them to their distinct roles: a feed-forward transition encoder with learnable action queries for inverse dynamics, and a causal, action-conditioned video generator for forward dynamics. By controlling information access and optimizing both dynamics end-to-end through a compact bottleneck, O$^{2}$LaF learns transferable actions from unlabeled videos. Across navigation and robotic manipulation, O$^{2}$LaF sets a new state of the art in few-shot action probing and enables stronger zero-shot action transfer across visual contexts and embodiments. Beyond generative video priors, we further extend our framework to predictive representation priors such as V-JEPA2, achieving competitive performance. Our findings suggest a broader paradigm for latent-action learning: repurposing pretrained video models to discover transferable actions and predict their consequences.

paper.paper_abstract: Collecting and labeling inertial measurement unit (IMU) data for human activity recognition (HAR) is expensive, and models trained on one group of subjects often fail to generalize to unseen individuals. Even with balanced data, classifiers struggle to distinguish dynamically similar activity classes and benefit from targeted augmentation. We explore whether synthetic IMU data generated in the representation space of a pretrained biosignal encoder, Bio-PM \cite{b1}, can serve as a practical augmentation source. Rather than synthesizing raw signals, we leverage Bio-PM's frozen encoder to convert 10-second IMU windows into token embedding sequences and train class-conditional decoders in this space: (1) an autoregressive transformer decoder that predicts tokens sequentially, and (2) a diffusion decoder that learns the token distribution through a denoising objective. We analyze generation realism through distributional metrics and embedding-space visualizations, evaluate downstream utility through leave-one-subject-out HAR classification, and present a PatchDecoder for approximate raw waveform reconstruction. Our diffusion decoder achieves a Train-on-Synthetic-Test-on-Real (TSTR) macro-F1 of 0.68, demonstrating that generated tokens are realistic enough to train a classifier that transfers to real data. Combining synthetic-token augmentation with a 320-dimensional gravity-aware feature representation raises LOSO macro-F1 from 0.729 to 0.809 over a real-only baseline across 51 subjects on the WISDM benchmark, with statistically significant gains concentrated in the most challenging activity classes. These results demonstrate that high-fidelity generation in a pretrained encoder's representation space is achievable and practically useful for cross-subject HAR augmentation.

paper.paper_title: Depth Pro 2: Sharp and Temporally Consistent Metric Monocular Depth
paper.paper_abstract: We present Depth Pro 2, an approach to estimating dense metric depth for images and video at full resolution. By analyzing prior methods for monocular depth estimation, we find that they commonly trade off temporal consistency and boundary sharpness: multi-frame methods favor consistency, single-frame methods favor sharpness. To overcome this trade-off, we train a single, scalable network that processes both images and video and predicts depth maps at native resolution. Depth Pro 2 produces depth maps that are metrically accurate, sharp, and temporally consistent all at once, outperforming prior work in all of these dimensions. We release a family of models that define a new Pareto frontier in terms of metric accuracy, sharpness, temporal consistency, and runtime. We release code and weights at https://apple-aiml-research.github.io/ml-depth-pro-2/

paper.paper_title: EEG-Jev: A Unified Single-Pass Decision Model for EEG
paper.paper_abstract: EEG analysis spans choosing alternatives, judging statements, and rating ordered attributes, requiring calibratable probabilities with explicit meaning. We present EEG-Jev, a unified single-pass decision model for EEG. Given an EEG window, a question and an answer specification, one forward pass returns a typed readout: CHOICE gives a candidate distribution, NOUL a proposition probability, and SCORE an ordered-level distribution and expectation. One checkpoint is trained jointly and evaluated once on held-out splits of 35 public sources. Core raw outputs reach 54.08% balanced accuracy on Stieger2021 motor imagery, 70.45% on Sleep-EDF-SC sleep staging, 72.11% per window at threshold 0.5 on CHB-MIT seizure detection with 0.825 AUROC, and 1.700 MAE on 0-10 ds005292 pain ratings. Prior correction and temperature scaling lower negative log-likelihood from 0.766 to 0.606 on Sleep-EDF-SC and 0.166 to 0.019 on CHB-MIT, while direct readout cuts batch-1 latency from 122.43 to 63.11 ms (1.94-fold) against a matched-backbone generative comparator. Interactive demonstration and aggregate results: https://neuroimglab.github.io/EEG-Jev/.

paper.paper_title: Is 4 Bits Enough for EEG Sleep Staging? A Subject-Level Benchmark of MXFP4, NVFP4 and FP8
paper.paper_abstract: Staging sleep on a wearable device keeps the raw electroencephalogram (EEG) private and saves the energy needed to transmit it. It also requires small, energy-efficient neural networks. We benchmark 13 post-training quantization (PTQ) configurations, from FP16 to the block-scaled 4-bit formats MXFP4 and NVFP4, for five-stage sleep staging from single-channel Fpz-Cz EEG. We use Sleep-EDF-78 (78 subjects), subject-wise cross-validation, three training seeds, value-exact emulation, and per-subject paired statistics. All 8- and 16-bit formats stay within 0.45 percentage points (pp) of FP32 Macro-F1. With 4-bit weights and activations, an epoch-wise CNN loses 1.98 to 3.04 pp, and a temporal-context network loses at most 1.19 pp. A same-encoder ablation shows that temporal context explains little of this gap. At equal block size, NVFP4 outperforms MXFP4. The first layer, which quantizes the raw EEG, is the most sensitive layer in both networks. Keeping the first and last layers in FP8 brings both tested 4-bit formats within 0.48 pp of FP32. This recipe adds at most 2.1% weight storage, needs no retraining, and is equivalent to quantization-aware training (QAT) within an exploratory 1-pp margin. The 4-bit losses fall on the same subjects across architectures (Spearman correlation coefficient = 0.69 to 0.79), and they reduce N3 recall the most. On the nested Sleep-EDF-20 subset, NVFP4 with FP8 first and last layers again stays within 0.25 pp of FP32. Under MXFP4, however, the ranking of the architectures reverses, and FP8 first and last layers do not fully recover two of the three tested models. In our emulation, NVFP4 with FP8 first and last layers thus loses little accuracy without QAT in both cohorts.

paper.paper_title: Learning Neurovascular Codes for EEG-to-fMRI Synthesis
paper.paper_abstract: In this paper, we introduce Neurovascular Codes as shared EEG representations for fMRI generation. We first train a separate EEG encoder to predict each fMRI signal, learning target-specific temporal and spectral features from the same EEG window. After training, we freeze the encoders and project their concatenated hidden features into a shared neurovascular code. Conditioned on this code, stochastic interpolant transforms Gaussian noise into a vector of fMRI signals, allowing different responses to be sampled for the same EEG window. We evaluate our approach on eight public simultaneous EEG-fMRI datasets, including four resting-state and four task-based datasets with 61,646 volume-level pairs. Under within-subject and held-out-subject evaluation, our model improves average Pearson correlation over the strongest encoder baselines by 19.1% and 19.8%, respectively. The corresponding improvements over the strongest generator baselines are 18.8% and 47.9%. Beyond reconstruction accuracy, we also evaluate the generated signals using subject-identification classifiers trained on real fMRI. Our method achieves the highest mean accuracy among the evaluated generators. We hope that our work opens up new opportunities for cross-modal brain modeling.

paper.paper_title: EEG Decoding in Context: A Framework for Tuning-Free EEG Foundation Models
paper.paper_abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) decoding is a central route toward brain-computer interfaces for communication, rehabilitation, cognitive assessment, and neurological monitoring. Recent EEG foundation models have substantially advanced reusable signal representations, but their downstream use still typically requires a task-specific decoder, gradient-based adaptation, and validation-driven model selection. We investigate a complementary foundation-model paradigm based on in-context learning: labeled EEG recordings define the decoding task as context, and new recordings are predicted without updating model parameters. We first pair raw EEG features with a pretrained general-purpose in-context predictor. This direct formulation provides a promising starting point, but its performance remains limited and unstable and does not generalize reliably across EEG paradigms. We find that suitable context construction can address these limitations by improving the effective signal-to-noise ratio and exposing temporal and spatial structure. Building on this insight, we introduce a general framework that combines EEG-specific context construction with a frozen in-context predictor and a metric-based context adaptation mechanism, which matches each downstream task to an appropriate context representation without relying on validation data. Across ten datasets spanning seven EEG decoding paradigms, our method achieves the highest mean BAcc among eleven specialized and fine-tuned EEG baselines, without task-specific parameter updates or validation-based model selection. This framework provides a practical path toward tuning-free EEG foundation models in which adaptation is expressed through context rather than parameter updates.

paper.paper_title: NeuroMotion: Aligning EEG to Discrete Motion Primitives for Continuous Motion Decoding
paper.paper_abstract: EEG-to-motion decoding remains challenging because noisy scalp EEG is difficult to map directly to continuous kinematics. We present NeuroMotion, a framework that aligns EEG representations to discrete motion primitives for continuous motion decoding across heterogeneous paradigms, including full-body free movement, lower-limb treadmill locomotion, and upper-limb freewill reaching and grasping. A VQ-based motion prior discretizes continuous motion into reusable primitives that serve as both alignment prototypes and intermediate prediction targets. Prototypical and supervised contrastive objectives align EEG embeddings to motion-derived prototypes and organize them according to primitive assignments. An E2M Transformer predicts motion-code sequences from the learned EEG representations, while a final geometric refinement stage improves continuous trajectory reconstruction through motion-level training. Under a last-session test protocol, NeuroMotion achieves the best mean reconstruction performance among the compared EEG decoding baselines across all three datasets, with the clearest gains on full-body motion in both reconstruction accuracy and distribution-level quality. Multi-subject ablations further support the contributions of EEG-to-primitive alignment, token prediction, and refinement. Code is available at https://github.com/Liuyi2351433/NeuroAction.

paper.paper_title: Layer-Readout Interfaces in EEG Foundation Models: Predictive Accessibility and Cross-Dataset Transfer
paper.paper_abstract: Intermediate layers often outperform final layers when foundation models are used as frozen feature extractors, but the source of this advantage is unclear. We study this question in EEG foundation models by separating three factors: how representations are read out, whether intermediate layers provide predictive utility beyond the final-layer interface, and whether useful depth structure transfers across datasets. Across five models and three tasks, improving the final-layer readout consistently recovers substantial predictive performance, yet intermediate layers remain advantageous within frozen extraction. We also find that layers selected on one dataset remain useful on another across five dataset pairs and four task families, and that a compact set of source-derived task directions retains predictive value after transfer in sleep staging. Together, these results show that predictive utility varies across depth, and its usefulness depends on how representations are read out and transferred. More crucially, source-selected layers provide a reusable feature interface across datasets, reducing the need for target-side layer search while outperforming final-layer baselines on target datasets.

paper.paper_title: MAS-BIT: A Multi-Agent System for End-to-End BraIn-to-Text Decoding
paper.paper_abstract: Speech brain-computer interfaces aim to restore communication by translating neural activity into text, yet end-to-end decoders have historically trailed cascaded systems in accuracy. We introduce a Multi-Agent System for BraIn-to-Text (MAS-BIT), the first multi-agent framework for end-to-end brain-to-text decoding from intracortical recordings. MAS-BIT coordinates three specialized agents: a neural agent that interprets continuous neural representations, a phonetic agent that decodes soft phoneme posteriors, and an arbitration agent that integrates their complementary evidence with direct access to neural representations to generate the final transcription. The expert agents communicate with the arbiter through token-embedding-based latent communication, constructing continuous messages as probability-weighted combinations of token embeddings. These messages retain alternative token hypotheses and provide a differentiable interface through which sentence-level supervision jointly trains the neural encoders and specialized agents across participants. MAS-BIT achieves state-of-the-art end-to-end decoding performance on the Brain-to-Text '24 and '25 benchmarks, with word error rates of 6.929% on '24 and 3.606% on the '25 public test set (3.892% on the private test set). These results surpass the published BIT cascade on the '25 public set and narrow the gap on '24, without ensembling independently trained models or using external language-model rescoring.

paper.paper_title: SleepXA: Composing Pretrained Neural and Cardiac Foundation Models for Sleep Representation Learning
paper.paper_abstract: Physiological signals recorded during sleep provide synchronized views of neural, cardiac, respiratory, and other bodily systems, while preserving modality-specific information. Existing EEG and ECG foundation models already capture rich but distinct physiological structure, motivating an alternative to training a multimodal sleep model from scratch: composing existing pretrained models. We introduce SleepXA, a framework that uses synchronized polysomnography (PSG) to compose independently pretrained neural and cardiac foundation models. SleepXA combines pretrained EEG and ECG encoders with lightweight encoders for additional PSG modalities, and learns shared and modality-specific representations through sleep-guided alignment. We pretrain SleepXA on 9,230 overnight PSG recordings from three large cohorts and evaluate it on 27 downstream tasks spanning sleep representation, clinical and disease prediction, and daytime physiological transfer. SleepXA ranks among the top two methods on 22 of 27 tasks. Controlled experiments further show consistent benefits across sensor configurations and EEG-ECG backbone choices, while pretrained initialization outperforms architecture-matched training from scratch and SleepXA surpasses alternative multimodal composition strategies. These results suggest that synchronized multimodal physiology can serve as a natural interface for composing existing physiological foundation models, yielding reusable representations that extend beyond sleep to clinical and daytime physiological settings.

paper.paper_title: Denoised but Not Improved: What EEG Denoising Does to a Downstream Task
paper.paper_abstract: Scalp electroencephalography (EEG) is routinely denoised before it reaches a downstream model, and the denoising literature scores a method by how closely its output matches a clean reference waveform. That reference does not exist for real scalp recordings: it is synthesized by adding artifact templates to signals merely presumed clean, and even an exact separation would return cortical activity blurred by volume conduction rather than the activity itself. Fidelity to it is therefore an unvalidatable objective, and whether it predicts any downstream benefit has gone largely unexamined. We report an audit that examines it. Holding a seizure-detection pipeline fixed and varying only the preprocessing stage, we find that five standard denoising methods, spanning analytic, cross-channel and supervised deep families, all fail to improve on the unprocessed signal, and most degrade it. To say what such a stage must instead do, we formalize a label-only, classifier-free probe that reads it by the separability geometry it induces on task-relevant features, decomposing any change into a between-class distance and a within-class scatter term. On a transform that does improve the task, the probe attributes the entire gain to a roughly one-quarter reduction of within-class scatter, with class separation statistically unchanged. What a downstream model benefits from is therefore variance suppression on task-relevant structure, which waveform-fidelity metrics neither measure nor reward.

paper.paper_title: PhyMind: Physics-Informed Masked Autoencoding for EEG Foundation Models
paper.paper_abstract: EEG foundation models are pre-trained almost exclusively with masked reconstruction through a free-form decoder, sometimes with hand-crafted spectral targets added, as in MANAS-2. We study what happens when that decoder is replaced by a generative forward model of EEG. PhyMind keeps a standard masked transformer encoder, but its decoder must explain the masked signal through 68 cortical regions, each driven by damped stochastic oscillators and an aperiodic Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process, projected to the recording's own montage by a fixed boundary-element lead field evaluated per derivation. Training combines masked reconstruction with a Whittle spectral likelihood, an oscillator-dynamics residual, a minimum-norm source prior and a penalised neural residual. In a controlled comparison (same encoder, data, steps and seed), the physics decoder produces encoder tokens whose spectral content is far more linearly decodable than with a masked-autoencoder decoder or with the MANAS-2 objective: mean R^2 on a token-level spectral probe with amplitude-normalised targets is 0.67/0.77/0.77 on three datasets, against 0.24/0.50/0.50 (MAE) and 0.48/0.67/0.66 (MANAS-2 objective), approaching the released 92.8M-parameter MANAS-2 (0.71/0.81/0.80). Downstream gains in the controlled setting are small (four-task mean balanced accuracy 56.6 vs. 53.8 for MAE frozen, 63.8 vs. 62.7 fine-tuned). Region-level features from the physics decoder raise frozen four-class motor-imagery accuracy by 7-14 points, so a 7.2M-parameter model pre-trained on 3k hours of open EEG is comparable to the released MANAS-2 with frozen features (63.0 vs. 61.6). After full fine-tuning, MANAS-2 remains better (66.8 vs. 65.4 for our best model). The inferred sources do not reproduce the lateralisation that a classical inverse solution finds in motor imagery, so we do not claim anatomical interpretability. Code and weights are released.
